name: Spanish Squat Isometric Hold
purpose: Patellar tendon pain relief and quadriceps isometric load without high joint friction.
instructions: Loop a heavy resistance band around an anchor and behind both knees just below the joint line.
Step back so there is substantial forward tension on the band with shins vertical.
Squat down to roughly 70-80 degrees of knee flexion, maintaining upright posture.
Hold the isometric position without allowing knees to drift forward beyond toes.
Breathe rhythmically throughout the hold, then slowly stand up.
precautions: Keep shins as vertical as possible to offload patellofemoral compressive force.
Do not push into sharp pinching pain; back off angle if discomfort exceeds 3/10.
verified_sources: Rio et al. (2015), British Journal of Sports Medicine: Isometric exercise induces analgesia and reduces inhibition in patellar tendinopathy
American College of Sports Medicine (ACSM) Exercise Guidelines

name: Supine Straight Leg Raise
purpose: Quadriceps activation and anterior chain control without patellofemoral compressive stress.
instructions: Lie flat on your back with the unaffected knee bent and foot flat on the floor.
Fully straighten the involved leg, dorsiflex ankle (toes toward shin), and lock the quadriceps.
Slowly raise the straight leg to the height of the opposite bent knee (about 45 degrees).
Pause for 2 seconds at the top, maintaining full knee lock.
Slowly lower back down with control and repeat.
precautions: Keep the lower back pressed flat against the mat to avoid lumbar hyperextension.
Ensure the knee stays completely straight during the raise.
verified_sources: American Academy of Orthopaedic Surgeons (AAOS): Rehabilitation for Patellofemoral Pain
Mayo Clinic: Knee Conditioning Exercise Guide

name: Terminal Knee Extension (TKE) with Band
purpose: Vastus medialis oblique (VMO) hypertrophy and terminal extension tracking.
instructions: Anchor a loop resistance band at knee height.
Step into the loop with the band positioned just behind the knee crease.
Start with the heel on the ground and knee slightly bent against the band's forward pull.
Contract your thigh muscle to press the knee back into full extension.
Hold the squeeze for 2 seconds, then slowly return to the slight bend.
precautions: Do not snap or hyperextend the knee forcibly; emphasize a controlled muscular squeeze.
verified_sources: National Strength and Conditioning Association (NSCA): Corrective Exercise Strategies
AAOS Rehabilitation Guidelines

name: Wall Slide Partial Squat
purpose: Controlled closed-chain quadriceps loading through safe partial range of motion.
instructions: Stand with back flat against a smooth wall, feet shoulder-width apart and roughly 18 inches out.
Slowly slide down the wall until knees reach no more than 45-60 degrees flexion.
Hold the bottom position for 3 seconds.
Drive through heels to slide back up to standing.
precautions: Never slide past 60 degrees during early rehab to avoid excessive patellar shear.
Keep knees aligned directly over second toes without collapsing inward.
verified_sources: ACSM Guidelines for Exercise Testing and Prescription
AAOS Knee Exercise Program

name: Prone Y-T-W Scapular Raises
purpose: Lower trapezius, middle trapezius, and posterior rotator cuff activation to stabilize scapulohumeral rhythm.
instructions: Lie face down on a mat or bench with arms extended.
Raise arms at 45 degrees forming a 'Y' with thumbs pointing upward; squeeze scapulae for 2s.
Form a 'T' with arms out to the sides; retract shoulder blades for 2s.
Bend elbows to 90 degrees forming a 'W'; externally rotate and squeeze mid-back for 2s.
Lower smoothly between each shape.
precautions: Keep upper trapezius relaxed; initiate movement from shoulder blades rather than neck shrugging.
Do not use heavy dumbbells; bodyweight or micro-plates are sufficient.
verified_sources: Kibler et al. (2013), Br J Sports Medicine: Scapular Dyskinesis Clinical Consensus
AAOS Rotator Cuff Conditioning Program

name: Side-Lying Dumbbell External Rotation
purpose: Isolated posterior rotator cuff strengthening to resist anterior humeral translation.
instructions: Lie on unaffected side with a small towel roll placed under the elbow of the involved arm.
Keep the involved elbow bent at 90 degrees, resting against your flank.
Holding a very light weight (1-2 kg), rotate the forearm upward toward the ceiling.
Pause for 1 second at top range without twisting your torso.
Lower slowly over a 3-second eccentric tempo.
precautions: Do not let the elbow migrate away from the body; keep the towel roll pinned.
Keep the wrist straight throughout the movement.
verified_sources: Reinold et al. (2004), Journal of Orthopaedic & Sports Physical Therapy (JOSPT)
American College of Sports Medicine Guidelines

name: Forearm Scapular Wall Slide
purpose: Upward scapular rotation and serratus anterior recruitment without subacromial impingement.
instructions: Stand facing a wall with forearms resting against it in a vertical parallel position.
Protract shoulder blades slightly by pushing the sternum gently away from the wall.
Slide forearms upward along the wall into a shallow 'V' shape.
Reach overhead as high as comfortable without shrugging shoulders or arching lower back.
Slowly return to start position.
precautions: Stop before the point of anterior shoulder pinching.
Keep rib cage pulled down and core engaged.
verified_sources: Cools et al. (2007), AJSM: Scapular muscle recruitment during rehabilitation exercises
AAOS Shoulder Conditioning Guide

name: Gentle Sleeper Posterior Capsule Stretch
purpose: Internal rotation restoration and posterior capsule mobilization for overhead athletes.
instructions: Lie on the affected side with shoulder and elbow both bent at 90 degrees.
Use opposite hand to gently press the wrist down toward the floor into internal rotation.
Apply very light pressure until a mild, comfortable stretch is felt in posterior shoulder.
Hold for 30 seconds while breathing deeply; do not force.
precautions: Ensure gentle pressure only; avoid causing sharp pinching in the front of the joint.
verified_sources: Wilk et al. (2012), JOSPT: The Athlete's Shoulder Rehabilitation
Mayo Clinic Sports Medicine Guides

name: Quadruped Bird-Dog
purpose: Spinal stability, anti-rotation control, and multifidus recruitment with minimal lumbar compressive load.
instructions: Begin on all fours on a firm mat with hands under shoulders and knees under hips.
Brace core gently as if preparing for a light cough, maintaining neutral spinal curve.
Slowly extend right arm forward and left leg backward until both are parallel to the floor.
Hold the outstretched position for 3-5 seconds without letting pelvis tip or rotate.
Return to starting position with control and switch opposite limbs.
precautions: Do not hyperextend the lower back; the leg should not be raised higher than hip level.
Imagine balancing a glass of water on your lower back throughout the movement.
verified_sources: McGill, S.M. (2007), Low Back Disorders: Evidence-Based Prevention and Rehabilitation
North American Spine Society (NASS) Guidelines

name: McGill Modified Curl-Up
purpose: Rectus abdominis activation with zero lumbar flexion shear or disc extrusion stress.
instructions: Lie on back with one leg straight and the other knee bent with foot on the floor.
Place both hands palms down under the lumbar spine to preserve natural inward curve.
Lift only head and shoulders slightly off the mat (clearing shoulder blades by ~1 inch).
Hold isometric contraction for 7-8 seconds while breathing continuously.
Lower slowly and switch bent leg halfway through sets.
precautions: Do not tuck chin aggressively or bend at the waist; the lumbar spine must remain neutral over your hands.
verified_sources: McGill, S.M. (1998), Clinical Biomechanics of the Lumbar Spine
American College of Sports Medicine Guidelines

name: Gentle Cat-Cow Segmental Mobilization
purpose: Restoration of pain-free segmental spinal flexion and extension within mid-range tolerance.
instructions: Start in a quadruped position on hands and knees with wrists under shoulders.
Inhale, gently dropping the belly toward the floor while lifting chest and tailbone slightly.
Exhale, gently rounding the back toward the ceiling and letting head relax downward.
Move slowly and rhythmically through comfortable pain-free range without pushing to extremes.
precautions: Keep movements slow and non-aggressive; avoid forcing end-range if discomfort occurs.
verified_sources: Mayo Clinic Back Conditioning Exercises
American Physical Therapy Association (APTA) Clinical Guidelines

name: Supine Glute Bridge Isometric Hold
purpose: Gluteus maximus activation and pelvic stabilization to unload compensatory lumbar erector overactivity.
instructions: Lie on back with knees bent at 90 degrees and feet flat, hip-width apart.
Engage abdominal brace and drive through heels to elevate hips until thighs align with torso.
Squeeze glutes firmly at the top without hyperextending lumbar spine.
Hold the top position for 5 seconds, breathing smoothly, then lower under control.
precautions: Do not arch the lower back to gain extra height; lift purely via hip extension and glute squeeze.
verified_sources: ACSM Health & Fitness Journal Rehabilitation Series
AAOS Spine Conditioning Program

name: Supine Submaximal Hamstring Bridge on Bench
purpose: Tendon remodeling and isometric bicep femoris recruitment at lengthened position without high eccentric strain.
instructions: Lie supine with heels resting on a low bench or sturdy box, knees bent at approximately 45 degrees.
Drive heels down into the bench to lift hips 2-3 inches off the ground.
Hold the isometric position without letting the pelvis rotate or drop.
Maintain continuous muscular tension in hamstrings for the specified duration.
Lower hips gently back down to floor.
precautions: Start with both legs; only progress to single-leg when pain-free during double-leg holds.
Do not perform sudden explosive lifts.
verified_sources: Macdonald et al. (2019), Sports Medicine: Hamstring Strain Injury Rehabilitation
British Journal of Sports Medicine (BJSM) Clinical Guidelines

name: Assisted Eccentric Hamstring Slider
purpose: Submaximal eccentric loading to lengthen fascicle length and build strain resistance.
instructions: Lie on back with socks or sliders under heels on a smooth floor.
Bridge hips up with knees bent.
Slowly extend knees, sliding heels away from body over a 4-second count until legs are nearly straight.
Lower hips to floor, pull heels back in, and reset bridge to begin next rep.
precautions: Use double legs initially; do not perform active concentric curl under heavy load during early rehab.
verified_sources: Askling et al. (2013), Br J Sports Med: Hamstring eccentric loading protocols
NSCA Strength & Conditioning Journal

name: Tibialis Anterior Wall Raises
purpose: Anterior compartment endurance and deceleration force absorption for shin splint recovery.
instructions: Stand with back and buttocks leaning flat against a sturdy wall, feet 12-18 inches out.
Keep legs straight and pull toes and forefoot up toward shins as high as possible.
Hold peak dorsiflexion for 1 second, feeling the anterior shin muscles contract.
Lower forefoot back to floor with control and repeat continuously.
precautions: Ensure back stays glued to wall; do not rock hips forward to create momentum.
verified_sources: Moen et al. (2009), Sports Medicine: Medial Tibial Stress Syndrome Management
ACSM Conditioning Guidelines

name: Seated / Bent-Knee Soleus Calf Raises
purpose: Soleus muscle and Achilles tendon heavy slow resistance with decreased gastrocnemius contribution.
instructions: Sit upright in a chair with knees bent at 90 degrees and feet flat on floor.
Drive through balls of feet to elevate heels as high as possible.
Pause for 2 seconds at top contraction.
Lower heels slowly over 3 seconds to a full stretch.
precautions: Perform with a slow controlled tempo; do not bounce through the bottom of the movement.
verified_sources: Beyer et al. (2015), Am J Sports Med: Heavy Slow Resistance vs Eccentric Training in Tendinopathy
AAOS Foot and Ankle Conditioning Program

name: Ankle Multi-Planar Alphabet Mobilization
purpose: Restoration of multi-planar range of motion and neuromuscular proprioception post-inversion sprain.
instructions: Sit comfortably with foot elevated and free to move.
Using the big toe as an imaginary pointer, draw each letter of the alphabet from A to Z in the air.
Make movements as large as comfortably possible while keeping lower leg stable.
precautions: Move strictly within pain-free boundaries; do not force uncomfortable end ranges.
verified_sources: Kaminski et al. (2013), National Athletic Trainers' Association (NATA) Position Statement: Ankle Sprains
Mayo Clinic Rehabilitation Guidelines

name: Cervical Retraction (Chin Tucks)
purpose: Deep neck flexor strengthening and suboccipital decompression to address forward head posture.
instructions: Sit or stand upright with shoulders relaxed and eyes looking straight ahead.
Gently draw chin straight back, as if making a subtle 'double chin', without tilting head up or down.
Hold the retracted position for 5 seconds, feeling a gentle stretch at base of skull.
Release back to neutral and repeat with rhythmic breathing.
precautions: Do not tilt head downward; the movement is purely horizontal retraction.
Stop if any dizziness, nausea, or visual changes occur.
verified_sources: Jull et al. (2008), Spine: Clinical Assessment and Management of Cervical Spine Disorders
AAOS Cervical Conditioning Protocol

name: Thoracic Extension over Foam Roller
purpose: Thoracic mobility restoration to reduce compensatory cervical extension strain.
instructions: Sit on mat with foam roller positioned horizontally across upper back (below shoulder blades).
Support back of head with hands, interlace fingers, and keep elbows pointed forward.
Gently lean back over the roller, extending thoracic spine without arching lower back.
Hold for 3-5 seconds, then return to neutral. Reposition roller 1 inch higher and repeat.
precautions: Always support the head with hands to prevent neck muscle strain.
Do not roll onto the lumbar lower back or cervical neck.
verified_sources: APTA Orthopaedic Section: Thoracic Spine Mobilization Protocols
ACSM Exercise Management Series

name: Side-Lying Clamshell
purpose: Gluteus medius isolated activation to control femoral internal rotation and knee valgus.
instructions: Lie on unaffected side with hips bent at 45 degrees and knees bent at 90 degrees, feet together.
Keep heels touching while raising the top knee as high as possible without rotating pelvis back.
Hold the peak contraction for 2 seconds, feeling the deep side glute working.
Lower slowly and repeat.
precautions: Keep hips stacked vertically; do not roll backward during the knee lift.
verified_sources: Distefano et al. (2009), JOSPT: Gluteal muscle activation during common rehabilitation exercises
AAOS Hip Conditioning Program
